title: The Sarbat Khalsa
hook: a gathering of the whole panth, rare today and much discussed

segments.voice: Yesterday, Takht Hazur Sahib at Nanded, by the Godavari. Your line was where he gave the guruship. What did you hand on, and did you hand it on well? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-four.

Who gets a say? A family planning a wedding finds out fast. So does a band choosing its name, or a club picking a captain. Somebody always asks: did everyone get asked, or just the loud ones? We've spent days on the Takhts, the seats of authority, and on the five Sikhs who decide for the community. Behind all of them stands a bigger idea, almost too big to hold. What if, for the gravest questions, the whole panth came together in one place, in the Guru's presence, and decided as one? Sikhs have a name for that gathering. It is old, it is rare today, and Sikhs argue about it with real feeling.
screen: `WHO GETS A SAY?` → `THE TAKHTS AND THE FIVE.` → `WHAT IF EVERYONE CAME?`

segments.voice: The name is Sarbat Khalsa. Sarbat means all, the whole of something. Sikhs hear the same word every time the Ardas, the common prayer, closes, when it asks for the good of all, sarbat da bhala. So Sarbat Khalsa is the whole Khalsa: all of us together. Now the history, told carefully. Sikh histories describe a time after the Tenth Guru, when Sikh bands were scattered and often hunted, and their leaders would meet at Amritsar at festival times. Tradition says they gathered before the Guru Granth Sahib, talked through what faced them, and made a gurmatta, a resolution taken in the Guru's presence. Once made, a gurmatta was meant to bind everyone, even those who had argued against it. That's the idea at its best: no single ruler, no single family, but the gathered panth and the Guru together. Then the hard part, and the reason it is so much discussed. Who calls a Sarbat Khalsa today? Who counts as the whole, when Sikhs live in many countries and belong to many organizations? Is a crowd in one place truly everyone? When gatherings have been called under this name in recent times, Sikhs have disagreed, sometimes sharply, about whether they truly spoke for all. Some hold that the Akal Takht should call it. Some want new ways for distant Sikhs to take part. Some think the old form fits the old days best. This path won't settle it. Under the argument sits the hope inside the word: that the Guru's community can still decide as one.
screen: `SARBAT: ALL, THE WHOLE.` · `MEETING AT AMRITSAR, BEFORE THE GURU.` · `A GURMATTA BINDS EVERYONE.` · `WHO CALLS IT, WHO COUNTS?` · then, large: `ALL OF US TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think how your group decides. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the last time a group you belong to made a big choice. Who was in the room? Now look for the one who wasn't, or who was there and said nothing. Don't fix it. Then picture the whole group sitting in a circle, that person included, every voice given room. Stay with that picture until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Sarbat Khalsa. The whole Khalsa gathered in the Guru's presence to decide as one; rare today, and much discussed. Today's word.
Your line: all of us together. Today, before your group makes a choice, ask the quietest person what they think. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: A Sarbat Khalsa is a gathering of the Sikh community before the Guru Granth Sahib to pass a gurmatta, a binding resolution; gatherings under this name are rare today and their authority is debated among Sikhs.
